newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris blast revives memories of 1995 bomb wave.
newsitem.headline: Paris blast revives memories of 1995 bomb wave.

text.p: A crack like a gunshot that signalled the bombing of an underground train on Tuesday revived the fears Parisians lived with during 1995 when a Moslem fundamentalist bombing campaign brought terror to the streets.
Two passengers were killed and dozens injured on Tuesday by a gas canister bomb that ripped through a carriage of a crowded commuter train at the Port Royal station.
In July 1995, just two stations away at the Saint-Michel Metro station, eight people were killed in an attack attributed to Algerian Islamic extremists.

Passengers and passers-by said Tuesday's blast instantly recalled their fears over the attacks on trains and in public places last year that were blamed on Algerian militants angry at French support for its military government.
"I thought immediately of that," said Remy Jiemza, 20, a student who was on the train when the bomb went off. "I don't know if I'll be able to take the train to my classes tomorrow."

Jiemza and others said the sharp crack was followed by a massive black cloud of smoke which poured out of the train and into the open-roofed Port Royal RER regional express railway station near Paris' Latin Quarter.
The smoke soon hung in a huge column over the station.
"There were women crying, there was panic everywhere. Smoke filled the air and everyone was suffocating," Jiemza said.
An American walking past heard the explosion and raced to the railing overlooking the station below.
"I could see people running up the stairs, fleeing the train. There were people pouring out, falling down, bleeding, in shock," said the man, who declined to give his name.

Rescue officials said the first alarm was received shortly after six p.m. (1700 gmt). A witness said a policeman was on the scene within one minute but could only look down the stairway into the station in horror as passengers fled.
Ambulances began arriving within 10 minutes in what became a well-oiled routine in the French capital last year.
An hour later, a dozen police buses and dozens of patrol cars were parked outside the station along the wide Boulevard Montparnasse and the area was sealed off.
Three hours later, ambulances were still leaving the scene under steady drizzle but rescue workers said all the seriously wounded had been evacuated long ago to area hospitals.
The lightly injured were treated near the scene of the blast in a university canteen, quickly transformed into a makeshift first aid station.
